passages.happening:
The Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover, is near. The chief priests and scribes are looking for a way to put Jesus to death, “for they feared the people” (verse 2).

“Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve” (verse 3). Judas goes to the chief priests and the temple officers and talks with them about how he might hand Jesus over. They are delighted and agree to pay him. He agrees, and starts looking for a chance to betray Jesus “in the absence of a crowd” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Passover was the great feast that remembered how God set Israel free from slavery in Egypt. For a week afterwards no yeast was eaten, so the whole time was called the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims. A feast about freedom, in a city ruled by Rome, could stir strong hopes, and the leaders feared a riot.

That is why Judas was useful. The leaders could not take Jesus in daylight, with the people hanging on his words in the temple (21:38). They needed someone who knew where he went at night.

Only Luke and John say that Satan entered Judas (John 13:27). Luke has not mentioned Satan since the temptation in the wilderness, which ended with the words that the devil “left Him until an opportune time” (4:13). Now that time has come. The temple officers were the temple's own guard, Jewish police under the priests.
passages.ot:
The betrayal by a friend recalls the psalm: “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9).

The Passover itself goes back to Exodus 12, when the blood of a lamb marked the houses of Israel and God's judgment passed over them.
passages.hard:
If Satan entered Judas, was Judas to blame? Luke holds two things together. Judas is not a puppet. He goes to the priests himself, he bargains, he agrees, and he looks for his chance. And yet something darker than greed is at work. Luke will say the same about God's plan: “the Son of Man will go as it has been determined, but woe to that man who betrays Him” (verse 22). In Acts Peter says that Jesus was handed over “by God’s set plan and foreknowledge” and put to death “by the hands of the lawless” (Acts 2:23). God's purpose does not make the betrayal innocent.

Christians explain how God's plan and human choice fit together in more than one way, and the traditions differ on it. These notes do not choose. All agree with Luke that Judas chose, and that his choice did not defeat God's purpose.
passages.asks: Judas was one of the Twelve. He had heard everything and seen everything, and still he sold his teacher. Ask what might be quietly pulling your heart away from Jesus, even while you stay close to him on the outside. Money was part of it for Judas. It is often part of it for us.

passages.t: A man carrying a jug of water, and a room made ready
passages.happening:
The day comes when the Passover lamb is sacrificed. Jesus sends Peter and John: “Go and prepare for us to eat the Passover” (verse 8). They ask where.

He tells them that as they enter the city, “a man carrying a jug of water will meet you” (verse 10). They are to follow him to the house he enters and ask the owner, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’ He will show them “a large upper room, already furnished” (verse 12). They go, find everything as he said, and prepare the Passover.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too, and the note on Mark 14:12-21 explains it. The Passover lambs were killed at the temple in the afternoon and eaten that night inside the city. Families from out of town needed a room, and people in Jerusalem made rooms available to pilgrims.

Carrying water was usually women's work. A man with a water jar would stand out in a crowded street. Jesus may have arranged this in advance as a quiet signal. With the priests looking for a way to arrest him, the place of the meal was kept secret even from the Twelve.

Only Luke names the two disciples sent: Peter and John. They will be together again, after the resurrection, in the first chapters of Acts.
passages.ot: The Law told Israel how to keep the Passover: a lamb for each household, killed at twilight, roasted and eaten that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs (Exodus 12:6-8). “And this day will be a memorial for you” (Exodus 12:14).
passages.hard: Was this the Passover meal itself? Mark, Matthew and Luke say it was. John seems to place Jesus' death on the day the lambs were killed, so that the meal came the night before. The note on John 13 sets out the ways scholars explain this: different calendars, John's meaning, or a meal shaped like the Passover. These notes do not choose. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover time, as the Lamb whose blood rescues his people.
passages.asks: Peter and John did the ordinary work: finding the room, buying the food, setting the table. Without it there would have been no Last Supper. Ask what plain, unseen work Jesus may be asking of you. It is often how his greatest moments are made ready.

passages.t: The cup, the bread, the cup: “do this in remembrance of Me”
passages.happening:
When the hour comes, Jesus reclines at table with his apostles. “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering” (verse 15). He will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.

He takes a cup, gives thanks, and says, “Take this and divide it among yourselves” (verse 17). He will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.

Then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it to them, saying, “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me” (verse 19). After supper he takes the cup in the same way, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
At the Passover meal people reclined, lying on cushions around a low table, leaning on one elbow. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, describes four cups of wine at the meal, with the story of the Exodus told over it. How much of that order was fixed in Jesus' day is debated, but it explains why Luke speaks of a cup both before the bread and after supper.

Only Luke gives Jesus' words ‘I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you’. He wanted this meal with these friends.

Luke's words over the bread and the second cup are very close to the words Paul passed on to the Corinthians: “This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me” and “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (1 Corinthians 11:24-25). Paul was Luke's friend and travelling companion. ‘Given for you’ and ‘poured out for you’ say that his death is for them.

What do the manuscripts show? Almost every Greek copy of Luke has the words as printed here, with a cup, then the bread, then a second cup. One early manuscript, Codex Bezae, copied in the 400s, together with some old Latin translations, stops after ‘This is My body’ in verse 19 and lacks the rest of verse 19 and all of verse 20. In 1881 two scholars, Westcott and Hort, judged that the shorter text was what Luke wrote. Most scholars since have judged that the longer text is what Luke wrote, and nearly all modern Bibles print it. A few still argue for the shorter one.
passages.ot:
‘The blood of the covenant’ goes back to Sinai, where Moses sprinkled blood on the people and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8).

‘New covenant’ comes from Jeremiah: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31). God promised to write his law on their hearts and to remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:33-34).
passages.hard:
What does ‘This is My body’ mean? Christians have read these words in different ways, and the disagreement is old and serious. The Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with, and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed churches teach that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and that believers feed on him by faith. Many Baptist and other churches see the meal mainly as a memorial, a way of remembering his death as he commanded (1 Corinthians 11:24). These notes do not settle the question. Every one of these churches agrees that Jesus gave this meal to his followers, that it points to his death for them, and that it looks ahead to the kingdom.

Does the shorter text in a few manuscripts change any of this? No. The words over the bread and the cup stand in Paul's letter, written before any Gospel, and in Mark and Matthew. The meal and its meaning do not hang on one manuscript.
passages.asks: Jesus gave his friends a meal on the night one of them betrayed him and the rest deserted him. He gave it to people who would fail him within hours. Ask whether you think you have to be good enough to come to his table. And notice the words ‘I have eagerly desired’. Jesus wanted to be at the table with them. He wants to be at it with you.

passages.t: The betrayer at the table, and who is the greatest
passages.happening:
“Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table” (verse 21). The Son of Man will go as it has been determined, “but woe to that man who betrays Him” (verse 22). The disciples begin to ask one another which of them it could be.

Then, at the same table, they argue about which of them is the greatest. Jesus says, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. But you shall not be like them” (verses 25-26). The greatest must be like the youngest, and the leader like the one who serves. “For who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves” (verse 27).

They have stood by him in his trials. He gives them a kingdom, as his Father gave one to him, so that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom and “sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell of the quarrel about greatness earlier, on the road (Mark 10:35-45). Luke puts an argument like it here, at the Last Supper, minutes after Jesus has given them the bread and the cup. It is a hard thing to read. Even then, they are thinking about rank.

‘Benefactor’ was a title rulers liked. Kings in the Greek world took it as an official name: one of the kings of Egypt, Ptolemy III, was called Euergetes, which means ‘Benefactor’. A ruler might tax and bully his people and still have himself honoured as their great giver. Jesus says his followers must not lead like that.

The youngest in a household had the lowest place and did the serving. At a meal the guests reclined and the servants stood and brought the food. Jesus, the host, says he is among them as the one who serves. John tells how that night Jesus washed his disciples' feet (John 13:4-5).

The promise of thrones over the twelve tribes is also in Matthew (Matthew 19:28). Twelve apostles for twelve tribes: Jesus is gathering Israel again around himself.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knew what a king should be. When Rehoboam became king, the old men told him, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day”, and speak kindly to them, “they will be your servants forever” (1 Kings 12:7). He did not listen, and the kingdom split.

The kingdom given by the Father recalls Daniel's vision, where the kingdom is given to the Son of Man and also to “the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:18).
passages.hard: Is Jesus against leadership? No. He gives his followers a kingdom and thrones. What he refuses is leadership that uses people. In his kingdom the one who leads is the one who serves, and the model is Jesus himself, who will give his life the next day. Christians and churches have often failed here, and those who lead in the church today stand first under this word.
passages.asks: The disciples argued about greatness at the most holy meal of their lives. Ask where you are still keeping score: at work, at home, in church. Then ask whom you could serve this week in a way no one will notice or thank you for. That is the place Jesus chose for himself.

passages.happening:
Jesus turns to Peter. “Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift each of you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (verses 31-32).

‘Lord,’ Peter answers, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death” (verse 33). Jesus replies, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this. Wheat was sifted by shaking it in a sieve, so that the grain fell through and the dirt and straw were left behind, or the other way round. It is a picture of being shaken hard.

The Greek shows something English can hide. ‘Satan has asked to sift each of you’: the ‘you’ is plural. Satan wants all of them. ‘But I have prayed for you, Simon’: here the ‘you’ is singular. Jesus has prayed for Peter by name.

Notice what Jesus prays for. Not that Peter will not fall. He knows Peter will deny him that very night. He prays that Peter's faith will not fail, so that after the fall he will come back. And he gives him a job for afterwards: ‘when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.’ Before Peter has failed, Jesus has already planned his return.

It happened. On Easter Day the disciples will say, “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). In the first chapters of Acts, Peter is the one who stands up and speaks for the others.
passages.ot:
The prophet Amos used the same picture of God's people shaken like grain: “I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations as grain is sifted in a sieve; but not a pebble will reach the ground” (Amos 9:9).

Satan asking to test a servant of God recalls the book of Job, where Satan asks God for leave to strike Job (Job 1:9-12).
passages.hard: If Jesus prayed for Peter, why did Peter still fall? Because Jesus did not pray that he would not fall. He prayed that his faith would not fail for good. Peter's courage failed that night. His faith, in the end, did not. Jesus' prayer was answered in the turning back.
passages.asks: If you have failed Jesus, badly, and you think it is the end of you, read these verses slowly. Jesus knew Peter would fall before he fell. He prayed for him by name before he fell. And he spoke of his return before he left. Your failure has not surprised him, and it has not cancelled his prayer. Turn back. And when you do, your story may be what strengthens someone else.

passages.happening:
Jesus asks the disciples, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” “Nothing,” they answer (verse 35).

“Now, however,” he tells them, “the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag; and the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one” (verse 36). “For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment” (verse 37).

They say, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” He answers, “That is enough” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this. Jesus looks back to the times he sent his followers out with nothing (9:3; 10:4). Then they were welcomed and fed in the villages. ‘Now, however’: everything is about to change. The one they follow is about to be arrested as a criminal. They will face a world that treats them as it treats him.

The word for sword here meant a short sword or long knife, the kind of blade a traveller might carry on the roads. The disciples, it seems, already had two between them.

Two swords among twelve men would be no use for a fight against the temple guard, let alone against Rome. And Jesus' answer is short: ‘That is enough.’
passages.ot: The words Jesus quotes come from Isaiah's song of the suffering servant: “He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). A transgressor is a lawbreaker. The servant is counted among criminals, and prays for them. In Luke, Jesus will be crucified between two criminals (23:33), and he will pray for those who crucify him (23:34).
passages.hard:
Was Jesus arming his disciples? Readers take verse 36 in three main ways.

Some read it as a plain word about the road ahead. The time of being welcomed is over; from now on the disciples must provide for themselves and expect danger, as travellers then did.

Many read it as a vivid figure of speech: Jesus is saying that hard days are coming, and they must be ready for a world as hostile to them as it is to him. The disciples take him literally and bring out two swords. On this reading ‘That is enough’ is a sad end to a conversation they have not understood, like saying ‘Enough of that.’

Others tie the swords to the words Jesus quotes next: ‘He was numbered with the transgressors.’ A little band with swords lets him be counted among lawbreakers. At the arrest he asks the priests why they came for him “as you would against an outlaw” (verse 52).

These readings can overlap, and careful readers hold each one. What no reading allows is to make this verse a warrant for violence. A few hours later one of the disciples used a sword. Jesus said, “No more of this!” And he “touched the man’s ear and healed him” (verse 51). Jesus refused to be defended by violence, and he healed rather than harmed.
passages.asks: The disciples heard ‘sword’ and reached for steel. Jesus was talking about the cross. Ask whether you, too, hear Jesus' words through what you already want them to mean. And ask what it would look like to be ready for hard days the way he was: not armed, but praying.

passages.t: On the Mount of Olives: “not My will, but Yours”
passages.happening:
Jesus goes out, as he usually does, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples follow. At the place, he tells them, “Pray that you will not enter into temptation” (verse 40). He goes about a stone's throw beyond them, kneels down and prays, “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (verse 42).

“Then an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him. And in His anguish, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (verses 43-44).

When he rises from prayer and goes back to the disciples, he finds them “asleep, exhausted from sorrow” (verse 45). “Why are you sleeping?” he asks. “Get up and pray so that you will not enter into temptation” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew name the place Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives (see the note on Mark 14:32-42). Luke says only ‘the place’, the spot where Jesus went ‘as usual’. Judas knew it.

Luke tells the scene more briefly than Mark. Jesus prays once, not three times. He kneels. And only Luke says the disciples were sleeping ‘from sorrow’. Luke is gentle with them. Grief can make a person too tired to stay awake.

The cup is a picture from the prophets: a cup of suffering, of God's judgment on sin, which Jesus is about to drink for others.

Luke says his sweat became ‘like’ drops of blood. He may mean that it fell in heavy drops, the way blood drips from a wound. Some have suggested a rare condition, described by doctors, in which a person under extreme stress sweats blood. Luke does not say that, and his word ‘like’ leaves the question open. Either way, the point is the depth of Jesus' anguish. The word for ‘anguish’ is agōnia, from which English gets ‘agony’.
passages.ot:
The cup of suffering is in the prophets: Jerusalem had “drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17).

Angels strengthening God's servants is an old picture too. An angel touched the worn-out prophet Elijah and said, “Get up and eat” (1 Kings 19:5).
passages.hard:
Are verses 43 and 44 part of Luke? These two verses are missing from some of the oldest copies of Luke, including a papyrus called P75, copied around AD 200, and Codex Vaticanus from the 300s. They are present in Codex Sinaiticus as first written, in Codex Bezae, and in most later copies, and writers of the second century, Justin and Irenaeus, seem to have known them. Scholars are divided. Some think they were added early, to stress that Jesus truly suffered as a man. Others think some copyists left them out because an angel strengthening Jesus seemed to make him look weak. Many modern Bibles print them with a note or in brackets. Jesus' anguish that night does not rest on these verses alone; Mark tells of it too (Mark 14:33-36).

Why would the Son of God dread death and ask to be spared? The church's answer has been that Jesus was truly human, with a real human soul and a real human will. He felt horror at death and at the cup, as a real man would. And he freely gave his will to the Father's.

In Mark Jesus tells his friends, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death” (Mark 14:34). This passage also speaks to anyone who has known sorrow so heavy it felt like dying. Jesus did not hide that sorrow. He said it out loud, to his friends and to his Father. If you are in a place like that, you are not wrong to say so, and you should not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live.
passages.asks: Jesus' prayer has two halves, and both are honest. ‘Take this cup from Me’ is a real request. ‘Yet not My will, but Yours be done’ is a real surrender. Ask whether you allow yourself to pray the first half, and whether you can pray the second. Notice also how gently Luke speaks of the sleeping friends: worn out by sorrow. Jesus wakes them, and he does not stop loving them.

passages.t: A kiss, a sword, and an ear healed
passages.happening:
While Jesus is still speaking, a crowd arrives, led by Judas. He comes to kiss Jesus. Jesus says, “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (verse 48).

Those around Jesus ask, “Lord, should we strike with our swords?” One of them strikes the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear. Jesus answers, “No more of this!” And “He touched the man’s ear and healed him” (verse 51).

Then he speaks to the chief priests, temple officers and elders who have come for him: “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw? Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me. But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness” (verses 52-53).
passages.hearers:
Mark, Matthew and John all tell of the arrest, and the notes on Mark 14:43-52 and Matthew 26:47-56 explain it. A student often greeted his teacher with a kiss. That is what made Judas's signal work.

John tells us that the one who struck was Simon Peter and that the servant's name was Malchus (John 18:10). Matthew gives Jesus' words, “Put your sword back in its place” (Matthew 26:52).

Only Luke tells that Jesus healed the ear. The church has long held that this Gospel's writer was Luke, whom Paul calls “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). The last healing Jesus does before the cross is for a man who came to arrest him. Only Luke has the words ‘this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness’. They came at night because they feared the people who heard him by day.
passages.ot: Jesus' refusal to strike back fits Isaiah's servant: “I offered My back to those who struck Me” (Isaiah 50:6). And the arrest of an innocent man as though he were a criminal fits the servant ‘numbered with the transgressors’ (Isaiah 53:12), the verse Jesus has just quoted.
passages.hard: Does this passage settle whether a Christian may ever use force? Christians have read the arrest in more than one way. Some, in the peace churches, read it with Jesus' teaching to turn the other cheek (6:29) as a call to refuse violence altogether. Others read it as a word about this moment, and about the church's mission, which must never be carried forward by the sword, while they hold that governments may rightly use force to protect the innocent (Romans 13:4). These notes do not settle that question. All agree on what Jesus did that night: he refused to be defended by violence, and he healed rather than harmed.
passages.asks: Jesus healed the ear of a man who came to take him. Ask whether there is someone who has come against you whom you could treat with that kind of mercy. And ask where you are tempted to defend Jesus, or your church, or your side, by means he refused.

passages.t: Peter denies Jesus, and the Lord looks at him
passages.happening:
They seize Jesus and take him to the high priest's house. Peter follows at a distance. In the middle of the courtyard a fire is lit, and Peter sits down with the others. A servant girl stares at him in the firelight: “This man also was with Him.” Peter denies it: “Woman, I do not know Him” (verses 56-57).

A little later someone else says, “You also are one of them.” “Man, I am not” (verse 58). About an hour later another man insists, “Certainly this man was with Him, for he too is a Galilean.” Peter says, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” While he is still speaking, the rooster crows (verses 59-60).

“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (verse 61). Peter remembers what Jesus said, that before the rooster crowed he would deny him three times. “And he went outside and wept bitterly” (verse 62).
passages.hearers:
All four Gospels tell of Peter's denial, and the notes on Mark 14:66-72 and John 18 explain it. People from Galilee spoke with an accent that people in Jerusalem could notice. Matthew says it was Peter's speech that gave him away (Matthew 26:73).

Luke tells it his own way. In Mark the hearing before the council happens at night while Peter is in the courtyard. In Luke, Jesus is held in the high priest's house through the night, and the council meets at daybreak (verse 66). So in Luke, Jesus is near enough to see Peter.

Only Luke tells of the look. ‘The Lord turned and looked at Peter.’ Luke does not say what was in that look, and it is wise not to say more than he does. But the reader has heard Jesus' words a few hours before: ‘I have prayed for you, Simon’ (verse 32). The one who looked at Peter was the one who had prayed for him.
passages.ot: The Psalms know the grief of turning away from God and the hope of being brought back: “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit” (Psalm 51:12). And God says through Isaiah, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you” (Isaiah 44:22).
passages.hard:
Was Peter's failure the end of him? Luke has already answered. Jesus prayed for him before he fell, and spoke of his turning back (verse 32). On Easter Day the risen Lord appears to Simon (24:34). John tells how Jesus asked him three times, ‘Do you love Me?’, one question for each denial (John 21:15-17). In Acts it is Peter who stands up at Pentecost and preaches.

Peter wept. That is the difference between Peter and Judas in the story: one is brought back. The bitter tears were not the end. They were the beginning of his turning.
passages.asks: Peter said ‘I do not know Him’ to a servant girl by a fire. Most denials are like that: small, quick, to protect ourselves. Ask whether there is a failure you have stopped believing God could forgive. Then picture the look. It was the look of someone who had already prayed for you, and was going to the cross for you.

passages.t: Mocked in the night, questioned at daybreak
passages.happening:
The men holding Jesus mock him and beat him. They blindfold him and keep saying, “Prophesy! Who hit You?” (verse 64), and say many other things against him.

At daybreak the council of the elders, the chief priests and scribes, meets and brings Jesus before it. “If You are the Christ, tell us.” He answers, “If I tell you, you will not believe. And if I ask you a question, you will not answer. But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (verses 67-69).

They all ask, “Are You then the Son of God?” He replies, “You say that I am” (verse 70). “Why do we need any more testimony?” they say. “We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips” (verse 71).
passages.hearers:
The Sanhedrin was the leading council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders and scribes, with the high priest at its head. Luke does not name the high priest here; other Gospels call him Caiaphas (see the note on Mark 14:53-65).

The mocking has a cruel irony. They blindfold Jesus and dare him to prophesy, at the very moment his prophecy about Peter has come true in the courtyard.

Luke's hearing is short. There are no false witnesses, as in Mark. There is no tearing of robes. There is a question, and Jesus' answer. ‘You say that I am’ is not a refusal. It is a way of saying, ‘Those are your words, and they are true.’ The council takes it as a yes.
passages.ot:
Jesus' answer joins two Old Testament passages. Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, “Sit at My right hand.” And Daniel 7:13, where “One like the Son of Man” comes “with the clouds of heaven” to receive a kingdom from God. He is claiming to share God's throne.

The beating of the blindfolded Jesus fits Isaiah's servant: “I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle” (Isaiah 50:6).
passages.hard:
Was this a lawful trial? The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, gives rules for a court in a capital case: such a trial must be held by day, and a guilty verdict must wait until the next day. Scholars disagree on what that shows. Some think rules like these were already in force in Jesus' day. Others point out that the Mishnah was written down long after the temple fell, and may describe the ideal law of later teachers rather than how the high priest's council actually worked in the 30s. It cannot be used to judge this hearing with certainty. Luke, unlike Mark, has the council meet at daybreak, and he does not argue the legal point.

It matters to read this scene carefully. Luke names particular people: the elders, chief priests and scribes of that council. He does not blame the Jewish people. Jesus, his disciples, and the crowds who hung on his words were all Jews.
passages.asks: Jesus stays quiet under the blows and speaks plainly when asked who he is. He does not defend himself, but he does not deny the truth to save his life. Ask whether you are more likely to defend your reputation or to tell the truth about Jesus when it costs you. Peter, that same night, had chosen the first.
